beginner.headline: Four Planets in November's Morning Sky
beginner.brief: In November, four planets will appear in a line in the sky before sunrise. They are Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter. You can see these planets without a telescope. Mercury will be the hardest planet to see. Venus is very bright, so it is easy to find. Venus will be higher in the sky than Mercury. Mars and Jupiter will look very close together on 15 and 16 November. Choose a place away from bright lights, with a clear view towards the east. Wait about twenty minutes so your eyes can get used to the dark. The best time to look is about 45 to 60 minutes before sunrise.

intermediate.headline: Four Planets Line Up Before Sunrise in November
intermediate.brief: Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will form a line in the sky before sunrise throughout November. All four planets will be visible to the naked eye, so viewers will not need a telescope to see them. Mercury will be the hardest of the four planets to spot. It will look dim and remain near the horizon, the line where the sky appears to meet the ground. Venus will appear above Mercury and to its right. Venus, which reflects a high proportion of sunlight, is the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon. On 15 and 16 November, Mars and Jupiter will appear very near each other in the sky. According to astronomer Gideon Bendavid-Walker, the gap between them will be roughly the width of a finger held at arm’s length. The pair will appear near the star Regulus, and the three objects may look like a group of three stars. Viewers should choose a place away from light pollution, meaning artificial light that makes the night sky harder to see. They should find an open view of the eastern horizon and allow around twenty minutes for their eyes to adjust to the dark. The best viewing time is approximately 45 to 60 minutes before sunrise.

advanced.headline: Four Planets Form November’s Pre-dawn Parade
advanced.brief: November’s pre-dawn sky offers a diagonal configuration of four planets. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will be observable without optical equipment in the eastern to south-eastern sky. Of these four planets, Mercury will be the hardest to discern. As the smallest planet and the one nearest the Sun, Mercury is persistently caught in solar glare. Its visibility is confined to twilight, and it remains faint and low on the horizon. An unobstructed south-eastern view across a flat horizon offers the recommended setting for spotting Mercury. What makes Venus especially conspicuous is that only the Moon appears brighter in the night sky. Among the major planets, Venus has the greatest reflectivity, the capacity to send incoming sunlight back into space. Observers can distinguish Venus from nearby Spica by looking for a steady glow rather than the star’s twinkling. Mars and Jupiter will be in particularly striking apparent proximity on 15 and 16 November. According to astronomer Gideon Bendavid-Walker at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, their angular separation, the angle between their positions in the sky, will be just 1.2 degrees. He compares that interval with the width of a finger held at arm’s length. Near Regulus, the two planets may resemble a group of three stars. While Uranus will be setting in the west before sunrise, Saturn and Neptune will be visible for a time in the evening. Observers should choose a location away from artificial skyglow with a good view of the eastern horizon, allowing around twenty minutes for their eyes to acclimatise to darkness. The recommended viewing period for the planetary parade is approximately 45–60 minutes before sunrise.
